name: Evidence Extraction Tables
title: Evidence Extraction Tables
answer: Evidence extraction tables are structured grids that turn the prose of studies into comparable rows and columns. In literature review and evidence synthesis they record study design, population, setting, intervention or exposure, comparator, outcomes, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and risk of bias notes. For AI research the same tables capture model family, training data, task, evaluation metric, compute budget, and code or data availability. They are the working memory of a review, not the review itself, and they support meta analysis, narrative synthesis, quality appraisal, and later audit. A table is only as useful as its codebook, which defines each field and the allowed values.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables are structured grids that turn the prose of studies into comparable rows and columns. In literature review and evidence synthesis they record study design, population, setting, intervention or exposure, comparator, outcomes, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and risk of bias notes. For AI research the same tables capture model family, training data, task, evaluation metric, compute budget, and code or data availability. They are the working memory of a review, not the review itself, and they support meta analysis, narrative synthesis, quality appraisal, and later audit. A table is only as useful as its codebook, which defines each field and the allowed values.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Evidence extraction tables run on spreadsheets, relational databases, reference managers, and review platforms, with templates and controlled vocabularies to keep fields consistent. Teams may use a shared workbook for small reviews or a database with forms, validation rules, and version history for larger ones. AI tools and scientific models can prepopulate cells from PDFs, but the schema, the codebook, and the final check remain human owned. A site library with 135 research papers and 12646 extracted claims shows how quickly a table set becomes a dataset in its own right. Storage, access control, and backup matter because the table is often the only structured record of what was read.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work starts with a protocol and a pilot extraction form, then a small sample of papers is extracted in duplicate to test the fields and definitions. Extractors record exact quotes, page numbers, sample sizes, effect estimates, and any transformations, and they resolve disagreements by discussion or a third reviewer. For AI studies the same discipline applies to model details, datasets, metrics, baselines, and compute, because those fields are easy to misread or omit. AI assisted extraction can draft rows, but a person verifies each cell against the original paper and logs any change. The table is updated as corrections, retractions, or new papers appear, with version notes so the review can be reproduced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in evidence extraction tables begin with copyright, licensing, and publisher terms for the source papers, and with privacy rules when extracted data include human participants. Provenance fields typically record the source paper, page or section, DOI, extraction date, extractor, and any transformation, so a claim can be traced back to the original work. A site policy of linking to the original paper rather than a search tool reflects that norm, and the trace is what makes a large table set trustworthy. Risks include hallucinated values, misaligned units, double counting, outcome switching, and hidden bias in automated extraction. Teams manage these risks with audit trails, access controls, correction logs, and clear separation between raw extraction and later interpretation.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward living evidence tables that update as new papers, corrections, and retractions appear, rather than static appendices. AI assisted extraction, active learning, and human in the loop review are likely to make first pass drafting faster, while verification and codebook design remain the bottleneck. Standard schemas, persistent identifiers, and machine readable provenance will let tables move between review platforms and knowledge graphs. Multimodal extraction from tables, figures, and supplementary files is an active area, as is multilingual extraction for reviews that cross language boundaries. The likely result is not a fully automated review but a faster, more auditable table that keeps a person accountable for every claim.
